catalog_locator: p. 172 (PDF page 8), section 'Linguistic State of Obo Manobo' > 'Phonology', first paragraph; saved file the copy we hold, text layer
catalog_quote: Two studies on Obo Manobo phonology were identified. According to Olofson (2007), the language has 17 consonant phonemes— b [b], d [d], g [g], h [h], k [k], l [l], m [m], n [n], ng [ng], r [r], s [s], t [t], v [v], w [w], y [j]— and five (5) vowel phonemes a, e, i, o, and u, with no diphthongs. Word stress is placed on penultimate syllables. The language also has a glottal stop phoneme, and six (6) consonants are borrowed from Cebuano and Spanish, especially in proper nouns.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (text in lines 405-410; extracted text of PDF page 8 = journal p.172, section 'Linguistic State of Obo Manobo' > 'Phonology'): the quoted passage is present word for word, including 'Word stress is placed on penultimate syllables.' I read the whole Phonology section and the reference list. Reading of that sentence = fixed: penultimate syllable is correct as a reading of the source. Status 'statement reported second-hand only' is correct: (1) Gasing & Al-Saggaf 2025 is an archival/desk survey, not a description; (2) the sentence is attributed to 'Olofson (2007)', which the reference list (line 969) resolves to H. Olofson's review of Brainard's Karao Texts (PQCS 35(4)), an unrelated book…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress reportedly falls on the penultimate syllable (second-hand summary; no examples, no conditions given).
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned. Note from a primary source (Brainard & Vander Molen 2005 fn.4) that vowel and consonant length are phonemic and /a/~/o/ contrast only in the last two syllables, which a real stress description would need to address; the second-hand summary does not.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level implied ('word stress'); no discussion of phrase vs citation forms. The attribution 'Olofson (2007)' resolves in the reference list to a book review of Brainard's Karao Texts (JSTOR 29792632), i.e. the citation is garbled and the primary basis of the sentence cannot be traced; the primary phonology (Khor & Vander Molen 1991 ms, SIL archive 43450) is not cited by these authors and is not available online.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources refer to Obo Manobo [obo] = Glottolog obom1235 (also called Manuvu', Bagobo, Kidapawan Manobo, Obo Bagobo; dialects Kidapawan, Magpet, Arakan, Marilog). The SIL team's materials (Khor, Vander Molen) are based on the North Cotabato (Kidapawan/Magpet) side of Mt. Apo; E. A. Manuel's 'Manuvu'' is the Davao-side variety of the same language.
